title: Seed Germination Days by Temperature: Calculator + Table | Hacé Cuentas
h1: How Many Days to Germinate Seeds? Calculator by Temperature
description: Enter your plant species and soil temperature to get exact germination days. Includes a reference table for tomato, pepper, lettuce, carrot, and cucumber at 15–25°C.
intro:
Getting seeds to sprout reliably is one of the most frustrating challenges in gardening—and the culprit is almost always soil temperature, not technique. This calculator uses the thermal time model (Growing Degree Days) to give you a precise estimate of how many days your seeds need to emerge, based on the species and the actual soil temperature at seed depth.

The key insight: seeds respond to soil temperature, not air temperature. In early spring, a warm 22°C afternoon can coexist with 10°C soil just 2 cm below the surface. If you sow peppers into that soil, you get rot—not slow germination. Knowing your soil temperature removes all the guesswork.

This model is the same standard used by USDA Agricultural Research Service, UC Davis, Cornell, and commercial seed producers worldwide.
keyTakeaway: **Tomato at 20°C soil germinates in 7–10 days. At 15°C it takes 14–21 days — nearly twice as long.** Pepper, cucumber, and basil fail entirely below 13–15°C. Always measure soil temperature at seed depth (2–3 cm), not air temperature.

useCases.title: Back-calculating indoor seed-start dates for tomatoes
useCases.description: A gardener in a USDA Zone 6 region has a last frost date of May 10. Tomatoes need 6–8 weeks indoors before transplanting. The calculator shows tomatoes germinate in ~8 days at 24°C (a heat mat temperature). Adding 8 days germination + 52 days to transplant size = sow by March 11. Without the germination estimate, many growers start too late and lose 1–2 weeks of growing season.

useCases.title: Diagnosing a failed pepper flat in early spring
useCases.description: A grower direct-sows bell peppers in a cold frame in April. Air temperature is 18°C, but a soil probe reads 11°C—below pepper's T_base of 13°C. The calculator confirms: at 11°C, expected germination = none. The fix is either waiting until soil hits 16°C+ or using a heat mat indoors.

useCases.title: Quantifying the ROI of a seedling heat mat for lettuce
useCases.description: At an unheated windowsill (16°C soil), lettuce germinates in approximately 10 days. With a heat mat set to 22°C, it drops to 6 days—a 40% reduction. For a market gardener running 4 germination cycles per bench per season, that's potentially one additional succession crop.

useCases.title: Spacing carrot succession plantings for continuous harvest
useCases.description: In May (soil: 14°C), carrots take ~17 days to germinate. In July (soil: 22°C), germination drops to ~9 days. Knowing this, the gardener adjusts sow dates so transplant-to-harvest timelines stay consistent through summer.

useCases.title: Planning a school garden with predictable outcomes
useCases.description: A teacher wants students to observe germination within a 2-week classroom unit. The calculator at ~20°C soil selects fast species: radishes (4–6 days), beans (5–7 days), basil (7–10 days)—instead of parsley (14–28 days) or celery (14–21 days).

example.title: Worked example: Tomato at 20°C
steps: T_base for tomato = 10°C; thermal time requirement ≈ 80°C·days

explanation:
## Germination Days by Temperature — Quick Reference Table

The table below shows how many days each species takes to germinate at three common soil temperatures. These figures come from USDA and university extension data (UC Davis, Cornell).

| Species | At 15°C soil | At 20°C soil | At 25°C soil |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lettuce** | 7–10 days | 5–7 days | 3–5 days |
| **Tomato** | 14–21 days | 7–10 days | 5–7 days |
| **Carrot** | 14–21 days | 10–14 days | 7–10 days |
| **Bell Pepper** | 21–30 days | 14–21 days | 10–14 days |
| **Cucumber** | ❌ Too cold | 7–10 days | 4–6 days |

*❌ Too cold = soil below the species base temperature (T_base); seeds absorb moisture and rot rather than germinate.*

---

## How Germination Days Are Calculated

The calculator uses the **thermal time (Growing Degree Days)** model:

```
Days to Germinate = Thermal Time Requirement ÷ (T_soil − T_base)
```

- **T_base** = minimum soil temperature below which germination does not occur
- **Thermal Time** = total heat units (°C·days) the seed needs to sprout

**Tomato at 20°C example:**
- T_base = 10°C | Thermal time ≈ 80°C·days
- Days = 80 ÷ (20 − 10) = **8 days**

**Tomato at 15°C:**
- Days = 80 ÷ (15 − 10) = **16 days** — twice as long!

**Pepper at 25°C:**
- T_base = 13°C | Thermal time ≈ 90°C·days
- Days = 90 ÷ (25 − 13) = **7.5 days**

---

## Base Temperatures (T_base) by Species

| Species | T_base (°C) | Optimal Soil Range (°C) | Fails Below |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tomato | 10°C | 20–25°C | 10°C |
| Bell Pepper | 13°C | 24–30°C | 13°C |
| Lettuce | 2°C | 15–20°C | 2°C (but fails >30°C) |
| Carrot | 4°C | 18–24°C | 4°C |
| Cucumber | 15°C | 25–30°C | 15°C |
| Basil | 15°C | 22–28°C | 15°C |
| Spinach | 2°C | 10–18°C | 2°C |
| Bean | 10°C | 20–25°C | 10°C |

---

## Practical Cases

**Case 1 — Tomatoes indoors (Zone 6, heat mat at 24°C):**
Expected germination = 80 ÷ (24 − 10) = **~6 days**. With transplanting 6 weeks after sprouting and last frost May 10, sow seeds around March 19. ✅

**Case 2 — Carrots in cold April soil (10°C):**
Carrot T_base = 4°C | Thermal time ≈ 130°C·days
Days = 130 ÷ (10 − 4) = **~22 days**. Gardener expected 2 weeks and assumed failure at day 14 — seeds were still viable. ✅

**Case 3 — Heat mat vs. windowsill for peppers:**
- Windowsill (17°C soil): 90 ÷ (17 − 13) = **22 days**
- Heat mat (27°C soil): 90 ÷ (27 − 13) = **~6 days**
A heat mat saves 16 days per batch — critical for commercial transplant producers.

---

## Common Mistakes That Delay Germination

1. **Using air temperature instead of soil temperature.** Soil can be 5–10°C colder than air in early spring. Always use a probe thermometer at seed depth.
2. **Sowing warm-season crops too early.** Cucumber and pepper seeds sown below T_base don't just germinate slowly — they rot.
3. **Ignoring the upper temperature limit.** Lettuce enters thermodormancy above 30°C and refuses to germinate entirely, even in summer.
4. **Treating packet ranges as fixed.** A packet saying "7–14 days" assumes 20–25°C. At 15°C soil, that same seed may take 20–30 days.
answerSnippet: Tomato seeds germinate in 7–10 days at 20°C soil, stretching to 14–21 days at 15°C. Pepper takes 14–21 days at 20°C and 21–30 days at 15°C. Lettuce is fastest: 5–7 days at 20°C. Cucumber needs soil above 15°C or seeds rot. Formula: Days = Thermal Time Requirement ÷ (Soil Temp − Base Temp). Tomato base temp = 10°C; pepper = 13°C; lettuce = 2°C.

faq.q: How many days does it take for tomato seeds to germinate?
faq.a: Tomato seeds germinate in 5–7 days at 25°C soil, 7–10 days at 20°C, and 14–21 days at 15°C. Below 10°C (tomato's base temperature), germination does not occur. For fastest results indoors, use a heat mat to maintain 22–25°C soil temperature.

faq.q: How many days for pepper seeds to germinate?
faq.a: Bell pepper seeds take 10–14 days at 25°C, 14–21 days at 20°C, and 21–30 days at 15°C. Peppers have a base temperature of 13°C — at 13°C or below, seeds absorb moisture and rot rather than sprout. A heat mat at 25–27°C gives the fastest, most reliable results.

faq.q: Why does soil temperature matter more than air temperature for germination?
faq.a: Seeds are embedded in soil and respond exclusively to soil temperature, not the air above. In early spring, soil can lag 5–10°C behind air temperature. A bright 22°C afternoon might have 12°C soil at 2 cm depth — below pepper's 13°C base temperature, meaning zero germination. Always use a soil probe thermometer at sowing depth.

faq.q: What is 'base temperature' (T_base) in seed germination?
faq.a: T_base is the minimum soil temperature below which a seed accumulates no thermal time and will not germinate — no matter how many days pass. It is not merely slow germination; it is a hard threshold. Warm-season crops have high T_base values: tomato 10°C, pepper 13°C, cucumber 15°C. Cool-season crops have low T_base values: lettuce 2°C, carrot 4°C, spinach 2°C.

faq.q: Do seeds germinate faster as temperature rises indefinitely?
faq.a: No. Germination rate follows a bell curve: it increases from T_base up to an optimum, then drops rapidly above it. Lettuce enters thermodormancy above 30°C and fails to germinate entirely in summer heat. Tomatoes show reduced germination above 35°C. Hotter is not always better — this is why seeds sown in a hot, unventilated cold frame in summer often fail.

faq.q: How do I accurately measure soil temperature at seed depth?
faq.a: Use a probe-style thermometer inserted to the actual sowing depth: 0.5–1 cm for small seeds (lettuce, basil), 2–3 cm for large seeds (beans, squash). Take two readings: early morning (daily minimum) and early afternoon around 2 PM (daily maximum). Average them for the most representative figure. Avoid measuring immediately after watering with cold water, which temporarily lowers soil temperature by 3–5°C.

faq.q: How can I speed up germination without special equipment?
faq.a: Several low-cost methods raise soil temperature: (1) Top of refrigerator: the compressor generates 21–24°C surface heat. (2) Humidity dome or plastic wrap: traps warmth and adds 2–4°C above ambient. Remove immediately at germination to prevent damping-off. (3) Pre-soaking large seeds (beans, squash) for 8–24 hours in room-temperature water shaves 1–3 days off germination. (4) Black plastic mulch over outdoor beds raises soil 3–8°C. A dedicated heat mat ($20–40) is the most reliable option.

faq.q: Why do seed packets give a vague range like '7–14 days'?
faq.a: Seed packet ranges cover the widest realistic consumer scenario — variable soil temps, moisture, sowing depth, and seed age. The range assumes 'optimal' conditions (20–25°C, consistent moisture). At 15°C soil, a packet saying '10–21 days' for peppers may actually mean 30–40 days. The thermal time model this calculator uses provides a specific prediction for your exact soil temperature.

faq.q: Does seed age or viability affect germination timing?
faq.a: Seed age affects viability (the proportion of seeds that can germinate), not the speed at which viable seeds germinate. Old seeds produce sparse, patchy emergence — but the seeds that do sprout appear on the predicted schedule. If germination looks slow but seeds are old, the likely cause is low viability: half the seeds are dead, not slow. Test 10 seeds on a damp paper towel at the target temperature to check germination percentage before sowing.

faq.q: Are there seeds the thermal time model does not apply to?
faq.a: Yes. The model works for non-dormant seeds of annual vegetables and common flowers. It does not apply to: (1) Seeds requiring cold stratification (most temperate tree species, native perennials like lavender and columbine — need 4–12 weeks at 2–5°C first). (2) Seeds requiring scarification (morning glory, sweet peas — hard seed coat must be abraded). (3) Light-dependent seeds (many fine-seeded herbs must be surface-sown, not covered). For these species, the calculator estimates speed once dormancy is broken, not time from raw sowing date.
